reading.rtitle: The Night the Vessel Turned Around
paras: It was almost midnight in Sao Paulo and Teresa Nakamura was still at her desk. Her team was finalizing a sugar contract with a buyer in Alexandria, the third counter-offer of the week, and everybody wanted to sleep. While she was reading the delivery clause for the last time, her phone rang. It was the shipbroker, and he was not calling with good news: the vessel was going back to the anchorage, because the terminal had no free berth.

So the delay started at 11:47 p.m., and by then three things were happening at the same time in three countries. In Alexandria the buyer was sleeping. In Rotterdam the trader who owned the cargo was watching the same news on a screen. And in Sao Paulo Teresa was doing the only useful thing anybody could do: she was reading the clause that decides who pays when the ship waits.

The clause said the seller pays only if the terminal caused the delay. Nobody knew yet what caused it, so both sides stopped moving. That is a deadlock, and Teresa says a deadlock is never about the money: it is about the moment when neither side can confirm anything. While the two lawyers were arguing about the cause, the shipbroker was quietly asking the port for the berth log, and it was the port, not the lawyers, that ended the argument two days later.

The deal closed eleven days late, and nobody backed out. Teresa now reads that clause first, before the price, in every contract that crosses her desk. She says the lesson was not about sugar or about ports. It was about a sentence she uses in every briefing since that night: tell me what was happening when it stopped, not what somebody decided afterwards.
reading.source: A composite portrait of a Brazilian commodity practice, written for this lesson.

choices: To explain how sugar is loaded onto a ship.
To show how a deal freezes when nobody can confirm what caused a delay — and what a lawyer does inside that hour.
To argue that shipbrokers are more useful than lawyers.

items.situation: Tell me what she was doing when the phone rang.
tips: She was reading the delivery clause when her phone rang.
Two verbs, two shapes: the long one gets was plus -ing, the short one is past simple.

items.situation: Now say the same thing starting with while.
tips: While she was reading the delivery clause, her phone rang.
When it starts the sentence, while almost always goes with the long action.

items.situation: Three places, one moment. Say what each person was doing at 11:47.
tips: The buyer was sleeping, the trader was watching the news, and Teresa was reading the clause.

items.situation: Correct me. I say: 'While she was reading the clause, the phone was ringing.'
tips: While she was reading the clause, the phone rang.
The phone ringing is the short interruption, so it takes past simple.

items.situation: Now your own case. What were you doing when a client called you with bad news?
tips: I was reviewing a contract when the client called about the shipment.

items.situation: Tell me a negotiation of yours that stopped. What was happening when it stopped?
tips: We were negotiating the delivery terms when the quota changed, and everything stopped for a week.

listenings.text: I want to tell you about the worst hour of my career, because everybody remembers the decision and nobody remembers the hour before it. We were finalizing a contract at eleven at night. My associate was checking the numbers, the client was waiting on the other line, and I was reading the delivery clause for the third time. Then the broker called and the ship turned around. Here is what I learned that night. When something interrupts a negotiation, the first question is never who is right. The first question is: what exactly was happening at that moment, and who can prove it? While we were arguing about the cause, somebody with no law degree was asking the port for a document, and that document decided everything. The lesson is not humility. The lesson is that a fact beats an argument, and a fact is usually somewhere nobody is looking.

People imagine that big deals collapse because somebody says no. In my experience they collapse because nothing happens. I was advising a client during a long acquisition, and the two sides had already agreed on the price. We were finishing due diligence, the lawyers were writing the last version, and everybody was expecting a signature before Christmas. Then the regulator asked for one more document, and nobody sent it, because each side thought the other one was sending it. Six weeks later the buyer backed out. Nobody argued. Nobody sent an angry email. The deal simply stopped moving while everybody was waiting for somebody else. That is what a deadlock actually looks like from the inside, and it almost never looks like a fight.
